fields.independence_analysis: The two census assertions (a_002, 1850; a_009, 1860) are recorded on separate original documents created ten years apart by different enumerators visiting the household. However, for the specific fact of Patrick's birthplace, both rely on whoever was the household informant at each enumeration — most likely Thomas Flynn or his wife, though the informant is unidentified in both. Because the same household member almost certainly supplied the birthplace information in both years, the two census records are partially dependent for this fact: they share the same underlying knowledge base. The 1908 death certificate (a_012) is drawn from an entirely different informant — Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown — who had no connection to the household enumerations. It is therefore independent of the census group for this fact. fields.weighing_analysis: Three decisive factors favor the Ireland reading. First, informant proximity: the 1850 and 1860 census informants were almost certainly people living in the household at the time — Thomas Flynn or his wife — reporting a birthplace they knew from direct family knowledge at or near the time Patrick was a child. By contrast, the son-in-law James Brown reported in 1908, roughly 63 years after Patrick's birth, a fact he could only have known secondhand. A son-in-law is unlikely to have received specific information about his father-in-law's Irish origins; he is more likely to have reported the American state where Patrick had long resided. Second, consistency: Ireland appears in two census records taken a decade apart, providing a consistent pattern from closer in time to the event. Pennsylvania appears only once, in the latest-created record. Third, the immigration-origin confusion pattern applies directly: it is well-documented that informants on death certificates frequently reported the state of the deceased's American residence — or the most familiar American place associated with them — rather than their actual foreign birthplace. The defensible rationale is a combination of more error-prone source/informant (a secondary informant reporting 63 years after the event) and an uncorroborated single item on the losing side relative to the partially-dependent census group.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The dispute concerns where Patrick Flynn was born — Ireland (reported in both the 1850 and 1860 censuses) or Pennsylvania (reported on his 1908 death certificate). The fact matters because it speaks to Patrick's immigrant origins and, downstream, to identifying his parents: a Pennsylvania birth would suggest native-born parentage, while an Irish birth fits the immigrant family pattern suggested by the census household.

The 1850 census (a_002) lists Patrick, age 5, in the Schuylkill County household of Thomas Flynn, with birthplace Ireland. The 1860 census (a_009) lists him again in the same household, age 15, again with birthplace Ireland. Both are original census images recorded by enumerators who visited the household. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (a_012) states he was born in Pennsylvania; the informant is his son-in-law James Brown.

The Ireland reading is more reliable for several converging reasons. The census records were made when Patrick was a child living in the household, and the informant — almost certainly a parent or other household member — was reporting a birthplace they personally knew. The same fact appears consistently across a decade-long gap and two separate enumerations. The death-certificate informant, James Brown, was a son-in-law who had no firsthand knowledge of a birth in the mid-1840s; he was reporting a fact he was told — or guessed at — about an event that occurred some 60-plus years before he provided the information.

The reason the death certificate gives Pennsylvania rather than Ireland is well explained by the documented immigration-origin confusion pattern: informants on death certificates routinely reported the long-term American residence of the deceased rather than the foreign birthplace, especially when the deceased had lived in one American state for decades. James Brown's most familiar answer — Pennsylvania, where Patrick had spent most of his life — was substituted for a specific Irish origin he had no reason to know precisely. This explanation is grounded in the informant's epistemic position: a son-in-law reporting a birth he could not have witnessed, drawing on general family knowledge rather than specific transmitted information.

fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County censuses both record Ireland, while his 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate states Pennsylvania. Resolving this matters because the correct birthplace is relevant to identifying his parents — an Irish origin points toward pre-Famine or Famine-era emigrant parents, while a Pennsylvania birth would suggest the family had already been in America a generation earlier.

The census side is represented by two original federal census records. In 1850, an enumerator visiting dwelling 84, family 91 recorded Patrick's age as 5 and his birthplace as Ireland. In 1860, a different enumerator recorded a Patrick Flynn of consistent age in the same Thomas Flynn Schuylkill County household, again with Ireland as birthplace. The household informant on both occasions was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — a person (or persons) with direct, firsthand knowledge of where Patrick was born. The death-certificate side is a single original Pennsylvania state death certificate, filed in 1908, naming James Brown (son-in-law) as the informant for Patrick's personal particulars.

Ireland is the more reliable answer. The census household informant had firsthand knowledge: they lived through Patrick's birth and could report his origin without guessing. James Brown, by contrast, was reporting a fact about his father-in-law's birth — an event that occurred roughly 63 years before the death certificate was filed, in which Brown had no involvement and no direct knowledge. Two consistent recordings by a well-placed informant outweigh one later recording by a secondhand informant, even when all three source records are originals.

The Pennsylvania answer is best explained by the 'immigration-origin confusion' pattern (Appendix B): a son-in-law, who knew his father-in-law only as an established Pennsylvania resident and coal-country neighbor, would naturally associate Patrick with Pennsylvania — the only place he had ever known Patrick to live. When asked to supply a birthplace for a form he may not have considered carefully, Brown likely reported the place he associated with Patrick (Pennsylvania, where the family had lived for decades) rather than Ireland, a fact he may never have been told or may have forgotten. This is a well-documented failure mode for death certificates: informants reporting where the deceased 'was from' in a social sense rather than where they were literally born. There is no credible mechanism by which two independent census enumerators, at 10-year intervals, would both have erroneously recorded Ireland if Patrick had in fact been born in Pennsylvania.

fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County censuses both record Ireland, while his 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate states Pennsylvania. Resolving this matters because the correct birthplace is relevant to identifying his parents — an Irish origin points toward pre-Famine or Famine-era emigrant parents, while a Pennsylvania birth would suggest the family had already been in America a generation earlier.

The census side is represented by two original federal census records. In 1850, an enumerator visiting dwelling 84, family 91 recorded Patrick's age as 5 and his birthplace as Ireland. In 1860, a different enumerator recorded a Patrick Flynn of consistent age in the same Thomas Flynn Schuylkill County household, again with Ireland as birthplace. The household informant on both occasions was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — a person (or persons) with direct, firsthand knowledge of where Patrick was born. The death-certificate side is a single original Pennsylvania state death certificate, filed in 1908, naming James Brown (son-in-law) as the informant for Patrick's personal particulars.

Ireland is the more reliable answer. The census household informant had firsthand knowledge: they lived through Patrick's birth and could report his origin without guessing. James Brown, by contrast, was reporting a fact about his father-in-law's birth — an event that occurred roughly 63 years before the death certificate was filed, in which Brown had no involvement and no direct knowledge. Two consistent recordings by a well-placed informant outweigh one later recording by a secondhand informant, even when all three source records are originals.

The Pennsylvania answer is best explained by the immigration-origin confusion pattern: a son-in-law who knew his father-in-law only as an established Pennsylvania resident and coal-country neighbor would naturally associate Patrick with Pennsylvania — the only place he had ever known Patrick to live. When asked to supply a birthplace for a form he may not have considered carefully, Brown likely reported the place he associated with Patrick (Pennsylvania, where the family had lived for decades) rather than Ireland, a fact he may never have been told or may have forgotten. This is a well-documented failure mode for death certificates: informants reporting where the deceased 'was from' in a social sense rather than where they were literally born. There is no credible mechanism by which two independent census enumerators, at 10-year intervals, would both have erroneously recorded Ireland if Patrick had in fact been born in Pennsylvania.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

This matters because if a second Patrick Flynn of similar age existed in the county in 1850, the 1850 co-enumeration would be ambiguous as parentage evidence, and the entire case for Thomas Flynn's paternity would rest more heavily on the death certificate alone.

Three independent searches of the 1850 Schuylkill County census — FamilySearch (original image, 8 results examined), Ancestry (index, 12 results examined), and MyHeritage (nil result, broader search) — returned no such record. The FamilySearch and Ancestry searches are not independent of each other (Ancestry indexed the same NARA microfilm), but together they confirm that the indexed universe of 1850 Schuylkill County census records contains only one Patrick Flynn of matching age. No source, assertion, or log entry in this project documents a second candidate. The competing candidate was a prospective risk marker, not an evidential finding.

The question is whether the Patrick Flynn whose 1908 death certificate is in evidence is the same Patrick Flynn enumerated in Thomas Flynn's 1850 Schuylkill County household (a_001). The competing scenario is that the 1908 death certificate instead belongs to the other Patrick Flynn enumerated in Schuylkill County in 1850 — a child of age 6 recorded at household 197, a different family entirely.

This information came from James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who was reporting his father-in-law's parentage — secondary information, but information he likely learned from Patrick's family over the course of a marriage. The name Thomas Flynn is directly corroborated by the 1850 and 1860 census records, which show a Patrick Flynn of consistent age living in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County for a full decade. No evidence of any kind links the household-197 Patrick Flynn to a father named Thomas Flynn, to Schuylkill County in 1860, or to the 1908 death.

The resolution rests on independent corroboration: two census records (different years, different enumerators) establishing Patrick's decade-long residence in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household, and a death certificate from an independent informant that names Thomas Flynn as the deceased's father. The geographic anchoring — Schuylkill County throughout — and the matching father's name eliminate the household-197 Patrick as a plausible alternative and positively confirm the identity.

The son-in-law's naming of Thomas Flynn as father is internally consistent with the census evidence and carries sufficient weight to resolve the identity question.
